title: Deer scat
def: Deer scat is a pile of small, dark, oval or acorn-shaped pellets, often 20 to 50 together, that shows where deer have fed or bedded.
look: pellets about 1/2 to 3/4 inch (1.5 to 2 cm) long, often with a small point or dimple at one end
dark and shiny when fresh, dull and dry or crumbly when old
in winter pellets are hard and separate; on spring and summer greens they can clump into a soft mass
use: Fresh, glossy pellets mean deer were there within a day or so. Many piles near trails, food, and thick cover suggest a regular use area, and piles in a bedding area mean deer rest there. Use it with tracks, rubs, and scrapes, not alone.
not: Scat cannot tell you a buck from a doe or how big the deer is. Do not touch or sniff scat with bare hands; use a stick, and wash your hands after. Do not camp next to a latrine or fresh bear sign.
steps: Check freshness: shiny and moist means recent, dry and faded means days or weeks.
Look for more piles along a line to find a travel route.
Note nearby food (acorns, browse) and bedding cover.
Note the spot if you want to come back.
alike: Rabbit scat: round, flattened pea-sized balls, not oval with a point
Moose scat: same shape but much larger, about an inch (2.5 cm) or more, and woody
Elk scat: larger and rounder than deer, rare in New England

title: Deer tracks
def: A deer track is a split, heart-shaped hoof print made by two pointed toes, about 2 to 3 1/2 inches (5 to 9 cm) long.
look: two teardrop toes forming a heart with the point toward travel
two dewclaw dots behind the print in mud, snow, or when running
an alternating walking line, with hind feet landing in or near the front prints
use: The pointed end shows the direction of travel. Sharp edges and loose crumbs mean a fresh track; rounded, rained-on, or leaf-filled edges mean an old one. Many tracks in a line usually mark a travel route between bedding and food.
not: Track size alone does not reliably tell a buck from a doe. Do not follow a track onto land where you do not have permission.
steps: Find the pointed end to tell direction.
Check the edges for freshness.
Follow the line a short way to see if it joins a trail.
Look for scat, rubs, and scrapes along it.
alike: Moose track: same shape but over 4 inches (10 cm) long
Domestic goat, sheep, or pig: rounder toes; pigs leave dewclaws set wide
Turkey or dog: toes and claws, not two hooves

title: Deer rubs
def: A rub is a sapling or small tree where a buck has scraped off bark with his antlers, mostly in fall before and during the rut.
look: bark stripped from one side of a small tree, often 1 to 4 inches (2.5 to 10 cm) thick, from knee to waist height
pale fresh wood, shredded bark curls on the ground, and broken twigs
several rubs in a line along a trail, called a rub line
use: Fresh rubs mean a buck has used the area this season. A line of rubs often shows a travel route, and the rubbed side tends to face the direction he was coming from. Big rubs on thick trees usually come from mature bucks.
not: Rubs do not mean a buck is there now. Last year's rubs are gray and healed.
steps: Check if the wood is pale and moist (fresh) or gray (old).
Look for more rubs in a line.
Note which side is rubbed to guess direction of travel.
Check nearby for scrapes and tracks.
alike: Beaver chewing: tooth marks and chips, often cut through near the ground
Porcupine feeding: patches chewed high on trees, with tooth marks
Moose rubs: much higher and on bigger trees

title: Deer scrapes
def: A scrape is a patch of bare earth that a buck paws clear under an overhanging branch and marks with scent, mostly in the weeks before the rut.
look: a pawed oval of bare dirt, often 1 to 3 feet (30 to 90 cm) across
a chewed or broken licking branch about head height above it
fresh tracks and a musky smell in it when it is active
use: Scrapes are scent posts that bucks and does visit. A fresh, damp scrape clear of leaves shows recent use; scrapes along field edges and trails show travel routes. Many hunters watch them from downwind.
not: Do not walk through or touch a scrape; your scent can make deer avoid it. Do not assume a buck visits it in daylight.
steps: Check if leaves have blown back in (older) or the dirt is fresh.
Look for the licking branch above it.
Find tracks in the dirt for direction.
Set up downwind of it, using the scent cone in Hunt.
alike: Turkey scratching: smaller scattered patches with no licking branch
Squirrel digging: small holes, not a pawed oval

title: Reading deer sign
def: Deer sign is the tracks, scat, rubs, scrapes, beds, and browsed plants that deer leave, and reading it shows where they travel, feed, and rest.
look: trails and tracks between thick cover and food
scat piles, oval beds pressed in leaves or snow
use: Sign is strongest where several kinds come together: a trail with fresh tracks, scat, and rubs near food or a pinch point. Fresh sign matters more than old sign.
not: Do not scout through bedding areas during the season; you will push deer out. Respect property lines and posted land.
steps: Walk edges between cover and food and look for trails.
Check freshness of tracks and scat.
Look for rub lines and scrapes in fall.
Note what you find, then check the wind before you pick a stand.
